The researcher conducted a content analysis of newspaper articles published in the legacy print media to determine the differences between how Hillary Clinton and Donald Trump were portrayed during the 2016 presidential general election.

Specifically, the researcher examined articles published in "The New York Times," "The Washington Post," "The Wall Street Journal," the “Chicago Tribune," and the “Los Angeles Times" from September 5 until November 8, 2016. 5Understanding the frames set forth by the media will provide a framework that can be used by candidates when making campaign decisions in the future.

Even as social media allows candidates to frame and set their own agenda, largely bypassing traditional media gatekeepers, the legacy media agenda continues to influence politics in the United States.
Research shows the influence newspapers have in forming public opinion.
LITERATURE REVIEW In examining the literature for this study, several points of interest emerged.

This review of existing literature will begin with a brief history of women who entered the race for president of the United States and continue through a closer examination of the media coverage into past political contests.

Finally, Hillary Clinton and Donald Trump, both candidates in the 2016 presidential general election will be briefly discussed followed by a discussion of the theoretical framework of gender stereotypes and the media’s framing of political coverage.
The purpose is to better understand how the legacy media portrayed Hillary Clinton against her male counterpart, Donald Trump, using print articles published during the 2016 general election.

Although Hillary Clinton is credited as being the first woman nominated for president by a major party (Collinson & Lee, 2016), the first announcement from a woman running for president occurred in 1870.
Victoria Woodhull, running against Ulysses S.
Grant, became a pioneer for women navigating the political arena (Finneman, 2015).
Portrayed as both an advocate for women’s right and an object of spectacle, Woodhull had a talent for drawing attention to her political issues (Jones, 2009).

Ray (2001) observes the fascination with Woodhull, “as a visible public amalgamation of the 9woman and the citizen, as a performative creation of a new being, the New Woman, who inspired both hope and fear” (p. 46).
Woodhull's run is considered even more significant because it occurred before women had even been granted the right to vote.
However, being a pioneering suffragette, Woodhull argued women had the right to vote under the Constitution's Privileges and Immunities Clause before the House Judiciary Committee.
Even after the Supreme Court ruled against the issue in 1871, some women showed up to vote in the 1872 election and were arrested for doing so (Bohanan, 2016).
Attempting to unite the gender and racial equality movements, Woodhull helped form the Equal Rights Party and named Frederick Douglass to her campaign as vice-president.
However, Douglass did not wish to associate himself with the campaign (Bohanan, 2016; Peterson, 2017).
Although over one hundred women have vied for the highest office in the United States (Finneman, 2015), The Center for Women and Politics (2016) lists only fourteen as significant.
This list includes Woodhull, Clinton, and three recent and well-known Republican candidates, Elizabeth Hanford Dole, Michele Bachmann and Carly Fiorina.
Bohanan (2017) notes Belva Lee Lockwood, also running with the Equal Rights Party was the first woman to appear on official ballots with her 1884 presidential bid.
She received historical acclaim four years prior as the first woman admitted to practice before the Supreme Court of the United States (Radeska, 2016).

Lockwood began her activism early on as Dannett (1971) notes. "When Belva was twenty-four, she began teaching in her native town, where she had her first lesson in 10 the inequality of salaries established by the school code: she earned $8 a week while male teachers were paid twice as much or more. 'I kicked to the school trustees,' she is quoted as saying, 'I went to the wife of the Methodist minister.
The answer I got opened my eyes and raised my dander: 'I can't help you; you cannot help yourself for it is the way of the world'" (p. 41).
Shirley Chisholm, the first black woman elected to Congress in the United States, ran in the 1972 Democratic presidential primary where she earned 152 votes.
When discussing the Convention, Chisholm noted, "You can go to that Convention and you can yell, 'Women power!
Here I come!' You can yell, 'Black power!
Here I come!' The only thing those hard-nosed boys are going to understand at that Convention: 'How many delegates you got?'" (Bohanan, 2017, para. 26).
The first elected female of an ethnic minority, Patsy Matsu Takemoto Mink ran in the 1972 Democratic primary in Oregon.
Patsy Takemoto Mink served the state of Hawaii in the House of Representatives before winning 2 percent of the vote in 1972 (Center of Women and Politics, 2016; Bohanan, 2017).

Also included is Lenora Fulani, the first woman to have her name on the ballot of every state. “Representing the New Alliance Party, known for its "black-led, multiracial, pro-gay, and pro-socialist" stance, Fulani in November smashed another record, receiving 225,000 votes--the most ever for a female presidential candidate in a general election” (Wiley, 2017, p. 41).
Two women of note have also run in the vice president slot in major parties.
Geraldine Anne Ferraro was picked by presidential candidate Walter Mondale in his 1984 bid on the Democratic ticket.
The first female Republican vice-presidential candidate, 11 Sarah Palin, ran with John McCain in 2008 (Center for American Women in Politics, 2016).

Having both Hillary Clinton running in the Democrat primary and Carly Fiorina running for the Republican nomination may have increased how many perceive gender in the media's portrayal of presidential campaigns, but coverage into their campaigns was hardly without gender bias (Dittmar, 2016).
Throughout the campaign, statements made about and by male candidates were designated "locker-room" statements.
Arguably the best well known would be in regard to the 2005 recording of a conversation between Donald Trump and Billy Bush.

The conversation, in which Trump was recorded as saying "he could 'grab' women by the genitals because he's a television star" (Newman, 2017, para.2) was released August 2016 and quickly dismissed by many as "locker-room talk" (para.5).
June 2015 held another example when Senator Mark Kirk was reported characterizing Republican candidate Lindsay Graham as a "bro with no ho" (Bump, 2015, para. 2).

Also in 2015, Republican candidate Mike Huckabee said, in regard to transgendered women being allowed to use ladies' locker room, he wished he had been told he could have "felt like a women" in order to be allowed to shower with girls (Bradner, 2015, para. 2).
Although the before mentioned instances, although widely covered by the legacy media, directly came from the candidates themselves, instances also were generated by 12 the media itself.
A 2015 New Yorker cover portrayed male candidates in a locker room, omitting Fiorina with Clinton only allowed to peek through the door (Hemingway, 2015).
Anderson (2017) argues Clinton struggled with a gendered double bind that pits media coverage of her as both a frontrunner and a first-time candidate.
While in the past women running for President have been largely thought of as a symbolic gesture than a true contender, Clinton was designated as a frontrunner.
However, Clinton also received negative media coverage.
The New York Post printed a political cartoon in which a donkey was holding a crown over an inpatient Clinton's head.
Bernie Sanders, her opponent in the Democratic primary appears to place himself between the crown and Clinton's head.
Many thought this was the publications attempt to encourage voters to "stop the coronation" (Anderson, 2017, p. 530).
Politics has been an integral part of Hillary Clinton’s life.
She was a Republican who worked on Barry Goldwater's failed, presidential bid.
After enrolling at Wellesley College, Clinton said she came to realize her political beliefs were no longer in line with the Republican Party and stepped down as president of Young Republicans.
She continued assisting in other's political campaigns including the 1968 Democratic primary campaign of Eugene McCarthy.

However, she still did not wish to run for public office, choosing to stay politically involved in other ways. "I did not imagine then that I would ever run for office, but I knew I wanted to participate as both a citizen and an activist.

In my mind, Dr. [Martin Luther] King and Mahatma Gandhi had done more to bring about a real change through civil disobedience and non-violence than a million demonstrators throwing rocks ever could" (Clinton, 2013, p. 37).
Clinton met her future husband in 1970 while they were attending Yale Law School.
She writes in her 2003 memoirs a fellow student was attempting to persuade Bill Clinton to write for a student publication when she noticed he kept looking at her.
That prompted her to introduce herself and they married in 1975.
She became the first lady of Arkansas, thereafter, and then the first lady of the United States.
As the first lady of the United States, her husband asked her to lead healthcare reform.
Clinton attempted to reform healthcare but failed after being unable to get a Congressional vote (Clinton, 2003; Goldstein, 2016).

Clinton (2003) writes she believes part of the failure lay in her underestimating "the resistance [Clinton] would meet as First Lady with a policy agency” (p. 248). 14 However, as Goldstein (2016) observes, this failure helped mold Clinton into the more cautious politician she soon became. "The 21 months from the dawn to the demise of the Clinton health plan showed the first lady as the Washington neophyte that she was, overvaluing her own ideas, misreading power relationships, crusading for a complex plan that would have disrupted many Americans' health care.
She has not attempted anything as daring again" (Goldstein, 2016, para. 5).

Clinton began her official political career February 2000 when she formally declared her candidacy for Senator representing New York, a seat she won November 7, 2000, after a campaign waged against her many viewed as negative by four-term New York Congressman Rick Lazio (Clinton, 2003; New York Times, 2000).
Clinton achieved history as the first woman to ever hold that position in New York.
She served eight years and worked with other New York lawmakers to get federal aid to rebuild after the 9/11 terrorist attacks in 2001.
She also introduced an act which required drug companies to research how their medicines impacted the lives of children (Amadeo, 2017).
Clinton ran for the Democratic nomination in 2008 but lost to President Barack Obama.

Shortly thereafter, President Obama appointed Clinton as Secretary of State in 2009 where she took the lead on several issues including, the Trans-Pacific partnership (Dwoskin & Lakshmanan (2013), a free trade agreement between the United States and eleven countries that border the Pacific Ocean (Amadeo, 2017).

Clinton also pushed for United Nation imposed sanctions on Iran (Carroll, 2015) and called for the raid on Osama bin Laden's Pakistani compound (Clinton, 2014; Amadeo, 2017). 15 Clinton formally declared her candidacy for the 2016 presidential Democratic primary April 12, 2015 (Chozick, 2015).
She fought against a host of challengers.
Her biggest challenge was from Senator Bernie Sanders, but in the end, she prevailed and received the Democratic nomination for president in July of 2016.
She became the first woman ever to be nominated by a major party to run for president in the presidential general election (Healy & Martin, 2016a).
Clinton’s media coverage has been a quandary of sorts.
Typically, research has shown female politicians are framed in more of a feminine light than their male counterparts (Kittilson & Fridkin, 2008).
However, as Dimitrova & Geske (2009) observe, the media often portrays Clinton as aggressive, a personality trait more commonly associated as masculine.
In fact, after Clinton was observed in tears while campaigning for the 2008 New Hampshire primary, media outlets seemed unsure of how to cover the seemingly unheard of phenomena (Breslau, 2008).
Goldstein-Schultz (2016) observes stereotypes as thoughts children learn from birth.
Lippman (1921) observes stereotypes are often used as a substitute for thought.
One can allow the culturally defined stereotype to determine our thoughts on a particular idea without putting in a great amount of thought.
Kittilson & Fridkin (2008) theorize thoughts based on stereotypical information will remain until contradictory characteristics emerge.
Gender stereotypes involve perceptions of personality traits or domestic roles assigned to a specific gender (Planned Parenthood, 2018).
The media 16 often employ the use of gender stereotypes in its framing of political coverage (Dolan, 2009).

A plethora of research shows how a female political candidate's appearance is commented upon more often than her male counterpart (Gordon, Shafie, & Crigler, 2003; Fowler & Lawless, 2009; Hayes & Lawless, 2015).

Gordon et al. (2003) found participants were statistically more likely to mention the appearance of the female candidate versus the male in their experiment measuring the effects of negative political advertising.

In addition to this, the mentions of the female candidate's appearance were more likely to be negative while most of the comments on the male candidate's appearance were gaged to be of a neutral tone. "The difference in the rate of negative comments is striking: while five out of eighty participants made negative comments about the male candidate's appearance, twenty-one out of eighty participants made negative participants made negative comments about the female candidate's appearance.
Participants did not like her hair and thought she was 'dowdy' and 'not very powerful looking'" (Gordon et al., 2003, p. 42).

In addition, the researchers found comments regarding the male candidate's appearance often seemed to impact participant's comments on his character, i.e., "young, well-kempt and full of promises" (Gordon et al., 2003, p. 43), comments on the female's appearance were on that alone, not bleeding into her character.

Fowler & Lawless (2009) observe the female candidate in their study received more than 81 percent more coverage on personal traits (including appearance, mannerisms, personality, and marital and parental status) than the male candidates. 17 Female politicians are often held to the standard of traditionally female personality traits in media coverage that often has an effect on a voter.

As Huddy & Terkildsen, (1993) explore, the higher the level of political office, the more characteristics that are stereotypically male, i.e., aggressive and demanding, were needed in order to adequately perform the responsibilities of said office.

In addition, the researchers found voters participating in their experimental study were more likely to vote for a candidate possessing stereotypically male characteristics than stereotypically female characteristics.

Prior research into gendered personality traits categorize stereotypically male traits as including tough, dominant, leader, and competitive; while more stereotypically female traits include: soft, nurturing, weak, and sensitive (Kittilson & Fridkin, 2008).

While sometimes beneficial to women candidates, i.e., Kahn (1992) found participants described female candidates are more honest, it can also be detrimental as the same study found male candidates were considered to have more leadership abilities.
A study into media coverage of gubernatorial candidates showed 450 articles with mentions of female candidates versus 249 for male candidates in the same time period (Fowler & Lawless, 2009).
Gender stereotyping does not simply rely on personality traits.
Political issues are often characteristics as “male” and “female” issues (Huddy & Terkidsen, 1993; Dolan, 2009; Heldman, Carroll, & Olson, 2005; Kittilson & Fridkin, 2008).
While male candidates are more associated with “hard” issues, e.g., the economy or domestic relations, females are often associated with “softer” issues such as healthcare or education.
Scholars have identified such male issues as including 1) the economy, 2) 18 taxes, 3) domestic relations, 4) employment, and 5) defense.
Female issues include 1) education, 2) healthcare, 3) gay rights, 4) gender equality, and 5) care of the elderly (Kittilson & Fridkin, 2008).
Research has shown the media is more likely to publish female candidates’ stances on stereotypically female issues.
Kittilson & Fridkin (2008) found only 24 percent of articles have a woman candidate’s opinion on a male issue versus 42 percent for male candidates.
The same study showed 76 percent of articles showed the woman’s stance on female issues.

Kahn (1992) found, “Differences in coverage of male and female incumbents lead participants to believe that the male incumbent is more viable, a stronger leader, and better able to deal with military (stereotypically male) issues (p. 508).

In a survey conducted by Dolan (2009), she observed 53.6 percent of participants felt as if a woman politician would be better with education (a stereotypically female issue) and 52.2 percent of participants felt as if a man would be more effective at tackling terrorism (a stereotypically male issue).
Prior research also shows the amount of coverage is often greater for a male candidate in the United States than for a female.

Kittilson & Fridkin (2008) show how in the United States, where the majority of coverage focus on “male” issues, “continues to be significantly more common for male candidates than for female candidates” (p. 383).

Fridkin and Kenney (2014) created the Strategic Stereotype Theory to explore how politicians strategically use gender stereotypes to emphasize strengths while diminishing characteristics in various forms of communication to strengthen their chance 19 of political success.
They contend political candidates are forced by existing gender stereotypes to use said stereotypes in certain situations in order to increase the possibility of their political success.

Communication generally falls within two dimensions: communal which is seen as a concern for the welfare of others and agentic, described as more assertive and controlling (Fridkin & Kenney, 2014). “The communal and agentic norms are so pervasive that they produce dilemmas for women and men who pursue careers and jobs requiring that they act differently from the prescribed norms” (Fridkin & Kenney, 2014, p. 16).
Gender stereotypes do not portray women as effective leaders.
The reason being males are often thought to have such agentic characteristics with communal characteristics often assigned to women.
Traditional gender stereotypes mandate what many view as appropriate behaviors for men and women.

The Strategic Stereotype Theory hypothesizes female politicians employ the use of traditional gender stereotypes by focusing on traditionally male characteristics in some settings while emphasizing traditionally female in others, depending on the need at hand (Fridkin & Kenney, 2014).
However, the theory depends on the media to project the strategically chosen stereotypes employed by the politician.
A failure of legacy media to frame the politician using the strategically chosen stereotype often changes the voting public’s perceptions of said political candidates.
The researchers observe political messages melding with existing gender stereotypes resonate with existing media who often use the same traditional gender stereotype framing.

The result often becomes the media reinforcing of these messages and citizen acceptance (Fridkin & Kenney, 2014). 20 The researchers also observe media outlets will interpret messages through existing gender stereotype frames.
Because of this, they theorized candidates will largely focus on issues complementing existing gender stereotype frames.
They theorize this for two main reasons.

One, they observe male and female political candidates often focus on broadcasting their stances on a different set of issues and politicians conform to this from fear of possible damage caused to their political career.

To examine the print media’s coverage of the 2016 Presidential General Election, the researcher employed a multi-methodology analysis of newspaper articles printed in The New York Times, The Washington Post, the Chicago Tribune, the Los Angeles Times, and The Wall Street Journal from September 5 until November 8, 2016.

Newspapers were chosen based on circulation rates of more than three million for The Times (Ember, 2017), 63 million for The Washington Post (Moses, 2016), 2.3 million for The Wall Street Journal (Statista, 2016), 2.45 million for the Chicago Tribune (Statista, 2017a), and 2.36 million for the Los Angeles Times (Statista, 2017b).
Also considered was the large online circulation rates.

Pew (2017) notes The New York Times added more than 500,000 digital subscriptions in 2016, The Wall Street Journal added more than 150,000, and the Chicago Tribune added more than 100,000, a 76% increase.
Wimmer and Dominick (2014) suggest the content analysis is a useful tool in measuring content characteristics of media.
The content analysis allows one to make inferences regarding the content of material already in print.

To answer research question three, the researcher conducted a thematic analysis on the sample searching for themes relating to the candidates' appearance, spouse, family, and descriptions of their personality traits and behavior.

To determine themes related to the candidates' appearance, the researcher conducted a thematic analysis for mentions of the candidate's clothing, hairstyles, and makeup choices, the researcher also searched for mentions of Clinton's pantsuits and Trump's hairstyles.
While mentions of these specific descriptors were analyzed, the researcher left open the possibility to discover other emerging themes in regard to the 34 candidate's appearance.
Also analyzed was if the candidate’s age was mentioned and how it was described, i.e., elderly, old, youthful, young, and middle-aged.
In looking for themes relating to the candidates' spouses and families, the researcher searched the articles for mentions of their marital status, spouses, and familial mentions.
Also, mentions of the candidate being described in family terms, e.g., grandmother, grandfather, wife, husband, mother, father, sister, and brother were noted.

In consideration of the prominence of both candidates’ spouses, the researcher defined spouse mention as if the spouse was mentioned in direct correlation to the candidate’s campaign, e.g., Former President Bill Clinton explained his wife’s stance on certain political issues.
Finally, the researcher conducted a thematic analysis for stereotypically male and female personality traits.
Personality traits were defined using a plethora of literacy and a list on Planned Parenthood's website (Gordon et al., 2003; Fowler & Lawless, 2009; Planned Parenthood, 2017).

Typically male personality traits were non-emotional, passive, independent, aggressive, tough or thick skinned, competitive, experienced, strong, active, self-confident, hard, rebellious, reliable, motivated, and assertive; and female emotional, sensitive, quiet, graceful, innocent, weak, nurturing, self-critical, flirtatious, soft, accepting, compassionate, understanding, and shrill.
A list of descriptors was compiled and then categorized by traditional gender stereotypes as being positive or negative male or female themes.

The categories were determined by existing literature (Fowler & Lawless, 2009; Planned Parenthood, 2018 ).35 Although the researcher began the thematic analysis with existing themes as determined by previous literature, she was open to other emerging themes.
